query: Consider the following context: Temper embrittlement, characterized by a dramatic loss of ductility within a narrow temperature window, is ubiquitous in conventional alloys but is not reported in compositionally complex or high‐entropy alloy systems. In that context, which material can be used for ductile–brittle–ductile transition, and why?

generation.hypothesis: An AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy will exhibit a more gradual and reduced ductile–brittle–ductile transition than conventional steels when cycled through the typical temper embrittlement temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast, homogenized AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy with a predominantly BCC/B2 or FCC mixture and minimal segregation.
generation.intervention: In situ synchrotron or neutron diffraction measurements conducted while thermally cycling the alloy through the 250–600 °C range characteristic of temper embrittlement in steels, combined with mechanical tests (e.g., tensile or impact) at critical temperatures.
generation.conditions: Incremental heating/cooling steps over the 250–600 °C window, with standard atmospheric conditions and controlled strain rates during mechanical loading.
generation.structural_mediator: Stable multi-principal element solid solution that mitigates grain-boundary segregation or short-range ordering effects seen in simpler alloys.
generation.mechanism: Compositional complexity and lattice distortions distribute solute atoms more uniformly at grain boundaries, suppressing embrittling interfacial phases or segregations, thereby preserving ductility across the embrittlement-prone temperature range.
generation.predicted_outcome: Unlike conventional alloys displaying severe ductility loss (∼50–70% reduction in impact energy), the HEA is expected to maintain comparatively higher ductility across the embrittlement window and recover full ductility above it.
generation.baseline: Various high-strength steels typically experience a pronounced drop in ductility when exposed to temper embrittlement temperatures (~250–600 °C).
generation.boundary: Alloy compositions or processing routes that induce excessive precipitation or segregation may still degrade ductility, so maintaining a stable, compositionally complex matrix is crucial.
generation.uncertainty: Exact transition temperatures and quantitative ductility retention remain to be firmly established under varying processing and testing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Compare tensile or Charpy impact properties of the AlCoCrFeNi-based alloy to a conventional embrittlement-prone steel under identical thermal cycles between 250 °C and 600 °C, with in situ structural analysis of grain boundaries.
measurements: Charpy impact energy over the temperature cycle
In situ X-ray or neutron diffraction patterns to assess phase fractions and grain boundary segregation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA shows a similar degree of embrittlement as conventional steels (i.e., comparable sharp drops in ductility/impact energy) under the same conditions, then the hypothesis is disproven.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy or compositionally complex alloys provide opportunities for optimization towards new high-temperature materials. Improvements in the equiatomic alloy Al 17 Co 17 Cr 17 Cu 17 Fe 17 Ni 17 (at.%) led to the base alloy for this work with the chemical composition Al 10 Co 25 Cr 8 Fe 15 Ni 36 Ti 6 (at.%). Characterization of the beneficial particle-strengthened microstructure by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and observation of good mechanical properties at elevated temperatures arose the need of accomplishing further optimization steps. For this purpose, the refractory metals hafnium and molybdenum were added in small amounts (0.5 and 1.0 at.% respectively) because of their well-known positive effects on mechanical properties of Ni-based superalloys. By correlation of microstructural examinations using SEM with tensile tests in the temperature range of room temperature up to 900 °C, conclusions could be drawn for further optimization steps. Keywords: HEA, high entropy alloys, compositionally complex alloys, mechanical characterization

decision.trend: Over the last decade, multiple groups have studied compositionally complex alloys and high-entropy alloys (HEAs) with stable multi-principal element compositions. Early work on eutectic HEAs (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) showed good ductility from room temperature through 700°C without the sudden brittle failure typical of temper-embrittled steels. Subsequent studies on refractory HEAs (e.g., Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr) and NbTaTiV systems demonstrated consistently high strengths combined with ductility in the 600–900°C range, again with no evidence of a narrow embrittlement temperature window. Later investigations used advanced synthesis routes (e.g., high-pressure/high-temperature processing of Al0.7CoCrFeNi) to overcome the usual ‘strength–ductility trade-off’ in these alloys. All these efforts confirm that compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys avoid the typical grain-boundary segregation and short-range ordering phenomena responsible for temper embrittlement in conventional alloys, yet the exact mechanisms behind their apparent immunity to ductile-to-brittle transitions remain incompletely understood.
decision.unsolved: Despite evidence that HEAs do not exhibit the classic temper embrittlement of conventional steels, the microstructural origins that prevent the sudden ductility drop have not been conclusively established. Specifically, it is unclear how compositional complexity, lattice distortions, and local chemical homogeneity jointly impede the grain-boundary weakening that drives temper embrittlement in simpler alloys.
decision.lever: Perform real-time neutron or synchrotron experiments on a model HEA (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi-based) while it is cycled through the typical ‘temper embrittlement’ temperature window to probe local grain-boundary chemistry, lattice substitutions, and defect evolution at high resolution.
decision.why: In situ, high-resolution characterization will capture any subtle atomic or microstructural gradients that might form in the temperature range historically associated with temper embrittlement in steels, shedding light on the fundamental processes that appear to preserve ductility in compositionally complex alloys.
